summary: This informational memo specifies extensions to RFC 1795 that improve the scalability of DLSw, plus clarifications based on implementation experience.

plainLanguage.summary: Improvements to an older bridge so it can handle many more users.

subtitle: Scalability improvements for bridging legacy computer networks.

tldr.problem: DLSw v1.0 (RFC 1795) becomes inefficient in large networks because it requires many permanent TCP connections between routers and sends identical address-resolution packets individually to each peer, wasting bandwidth and consuming excessive CPU and memory.
tldr.mechanism: DLSw v2.0 adds multicast-based address resolution and on-demand TCP connections, using UDP for lookups and multicast when sending to multiple peers, while also defining halt reason codes for better error reporting.
tldr.outcome: Large networks can be built with DLSw without the resource constraints of v1.0, while maintaining backward compatibility with existing implementations.

facts.label: DLSw v2.0 TCP port for single session

today: RFC 2166 is Informational and describes DLSw v2.0 enhancements that were relevant in the 1990s for bridging legacy SNA and NetBIOS networks over IP. As these legacy protocols have faded from widespread use, DLSw itself is rarely deployed. However, the principles of using multicast instead of repeated unicast, on-demand connections instead of permanent links, and combining TCP with UDP for different traffic types remain relevant in modern networking.

sections.title: DLSw and Scalability Challenges
sections.content:
DLSw (Data Link Switching) is a protocol for bridging legacy computer networks (SNA, NetBIOS) over IP-based networks. RFC 1795 defined v1.0 of DLSw, but it has scalability problems. In large networks, particularly those supporting NetBIOS which uses heavy broadcast traffic, DLSw v1.0 suffers from multiple issues: requiring all peer addresses to be pre-configured (administrative burden), sending identical address-resolution packets individually to each peer (bandwidth waste), propagating NetBIOS broadcast packets over point-to-point connections (more duplication), and maintaining constant TCP connections between all peers (excessive CPU and memory overhead).

RFC 2166 defines v2.0 enhancements designed to be fully backward compatible with v1.0 while addressing these scalability issues using IP multicast capabilities.
sections.plainLanguage: The old system requires routers to know about every other router and to send the same question to each one separately. The new system lets routers ask their questions to everyone at once, using less network bandwidth.

sections.title: Core Scalability Enhancements
sections.content:
DLSw v2.0 introduces four main enhancements. First, single-session TCP connections replace v1.0's two unidirectional connections, reducing TCP overhead. Second, TCP connections on demand means connections are only established when needed for circuit data and are torn down after the last active circuit ends, eliminating the overhead of permanent peer connections.

Third, address resolution via UDP and multicast is the key innovation: instead of sending address-resolution requests like CANUREACH to each peer individually over TCP, v2.0 DLSw nodes send these requests to a multicast group (224.0.10.0 is the default). The IP network delivers the packet to all listening peers, avoiding duplication. Responses are sent back via unicast UDP, avoiding the need to establish TCP connections for lookups.

Fourth, NetBIOS broadcasts over UDP similarly uses multicast/unicast to propagate NetBIOS frames, avoiding the bandwidth waste of the v1.0 approach.
sections.plainLanguage: The new system uses smarter tricks: only talk to someone when you actually need to, broadcast questions to everyone at once instead of individually, and use a simpler delivery method (UDP) for questions instead of always using reliable connections (TCP).

sections.title: Message Transport Mechanisms
sections.content:
DLSw v2.0 uses three transport mechanisms: TCP/IP for reliable circuit data (LLC2 based circuits), UDP unicast for directed address-resolution responses, and UDP multicast for broadcasting address-resolution requests to groups of peers. TCP connections are only established when a circuit needs to be set up. When circuit data is flowing, TCP's bi-directional nature allows TCP ACKs to be piggy-backed on data, improving efficiency.

For address-resolution protocols in SNA and NetBIOS, the switch to UDP and multicast is significant. Address-resolution packets like CANUREACH_ex can be sent to a multicast address, and any peer listening on that group receives it. The multicast infrastructure ensures the packet is only sent where needed, unlike v1.0's individual unicast copies. Furthermore, RFC 2166 defines a block of reserved IP multicast addresses: 224.0.10.0 (default), 224.0.10.1-191 (user-defined groups), and 224.0.10.192-255 (reserved for future use).
sections.plainLanguage: Use the reliable mail system (TCP) only for important packages, but use the quicker broadcast system (UDP multicast) for notices that many people need to see at once.

sections.title: Halt Reason Codes and Diagnostics
sections.content: RFC 1795 had no way for a DLSw to tell its peer why a circuit was being dropped. RFC 2166 adds HALT reason codes to HALT_DL and HALT_DL_NOACK messages. These codes indicate the generic reason for the halt (using values 1-5: unknown error, received disconnect from end-station, detected DLC error, circuit-level protocol error, or operator-initiated shutdown) plus vendor-specific detailed codes. This improves diagnostics and troubleshooting.
sections.plainLanguage: When a connection is closed, the router now explains why, instead of just disconnecting silently.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility and Migration
sections.content: RFC 2166 v2.0 enhancements are designed for full backward compatibility with RFC 1795 v1.0 implementations. When a v2.0 DLSw encounters a v1.0 peer, it uses traditional v1.0 mechanisms (two unidirectional TCP connections, individual address-resolution requests). When two v2.0 DLSws connect, they exchange capabilities and use the new enhancements. This allows networks to migrate gradually, with v1.0 and v2.0 nodes coexisting. The capabilities exchange mechanism signals which version a peer supports, enabling proper interoperability.
sections.plainLanguage: New routers can talk to old routers using the old system, but when two new routers meet, they can use the smarter system.

references.text: Bradner, S., and A. Mankin, "Data Link Switching: Switch-to-Switch Protocol", RFC 1795, April 1995.
